query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During thermal or environmental exposure, localized segregation of Mg in the metastable solid-solution matrix promotes the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and interfaces, disrupting the continuity of protective oxides/passivation layers and thereby reducing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-processed, single-phase state.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight Mg-containing high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, supersaturated solid-solution microstructure formed by rapid solidification or analogous nonequilibrium processing routes.
generation.intervention: In situ high-temperature exposure and/or corrosive environment exposure, with at least one sample held below the predicted intermetallic nucleation threshold and another held above it, for a controlled range of times.
generation.conditions: Temperatures typically ranging from ~300 °C up to ~500 °C in air or corrosive environments for extended durations (tens to hundreds of hours), capturing the onset and progression of intermetallic formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Mg segregation at grain or inter-phase boundaries, leading to the formation of stable or metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: Once Mg-rich intermetallic phases precipitate, local depletion of Mg in the surroundings and the formation of brittle intermetallic networks undermine oxide scale adherence and/or overall passivation, promoting accelerated corrosion and oxidation compared to the metastable single-phase condition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Above a critical temperature–time threshold, in situ characterization will reveal nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallics, accompanied by a measurable decrease in corrosion and oxidation resistance. In samples prevented from intermetallic formation by lower temperature or shorter exposure, the single-phase microstructure is retained and environmental resistance remains relatively high.
generation.baseline: An as-processed state with minimal or no second-phase precipitates, characterized by a uniform, single-phase solid solution and stable passivation behavior.
generation.boundary: Exposure below the intermetallic nucleation temperature–time regime maintains the supersaturated solid solution and near-initial protective properties; crossing that threshold leads to intermetallic precipitation and degraded corrosion/oxidation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact precipitation onset kinetics and the role of environment (e.g., solution pH, atmosphere composition) remain insufficiently characterized; confirmation requires time-resolved structural and chemical analysis under service-like conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose two sets of identically prepared metastable HEA coupons—one near (but below) the predicted intermetallic nucleation temperature and one at a higher temperature—for a prescribed duration in an oxidizing or corrosive environment. Monitor phase evolution in situ by high-temperature XRD and/or transmission electron microscopy, and characterize corrosion/oxidation kinetics via weight change or electrochemical polarization measurements.
measurements: XRD scans to track appearance of new intermetallic peaks over time.
Electron microscopy and elemental mapping to detect intermetallic phases, their locations, and compositional changes.
Mass change or surface characterization (e.g., oxide integrity, thickness) to evaluate degradation over time.
Electrochemical techniques (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to compare corrosion resistance in reference and high-temperature–exposed specimens.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If intermetallic nucleation does not occur (i.e., no new peaks or precipitates) or if corrosion and oxidation performance is not adversely affected above the predicted nucleation threshold, then the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: We investigate the effect of alloying with scandium on microstructure, high-temperature phase stability, electron transport, and mechanical properties of the Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Out of the three model alloys, Al2CoCrFeNi adopts a disordered CsCl structure type. Both of the six-component alloys contain a mixture of body-centered cubic (bcc) and face centered cubic (fcc) phases. The comparison between in situ high-temperature powder diffraction data and ex situ data from heat-treated samples highlights the presence of a reversible bcc to fcc transition. The precipitation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries following scandium addition affects all systems differently, but especially enhances the properties of Al2CoCrFeNi. It causes grain refinement; hardness and electrical conductivity increases (up to 20% and 14% respectively) and affects the CsCl-type → fcc equilibrium by moving the transformation to sensibly higher temperatures. The maximum dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) of 0.014 is reached for Al2CoCrFeNi alloyed with 0.3 wt.% Sc at 650 °C.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. decision.trend: Early work on Al-based HEAs revealed that small additions (e.g., Sc) can trigger MgZn2-type intermetallic precipitation and shift phase transitions. Subsequent modeling and experiments on Al–Mg-rich lightweight complex concentrated alloys, especially under heat treatment, showed partial retention of solid solutions alongside brittle intermetallics, affecting mechanical behavior. More recent pressure-assisted syntheses achieve highly supersaturated single-phase Al–Mg–Li–Zn CCAs, but the long-term stability and the exact transformation pathways – particularly under service conditions that involve corrosion or oxidation – remain incompletely understood.
decision.unsolved: It is unclear precisely how these Mg-containing alloys transition from an initially metastable solid solution into intermetallic-bearing microstructures, and how these evolving phases impact protective oxide stability and corrosion/oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures. The kinetics of intermetallic nucleation and growth, and their interplay with passivation and environment, remain unresolved.
decision.lever: Use high-temperature in situ X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy under controlled exposure (extending into corrosive/oxidizing regimes) to compare microstructural evolution in matched specimens, one held near the metastable threshold and another at higher temperatures beyond the presumed intermetallic nucleation range.
decision.why: Real-time tracking of phase transformation and intermetallic precipitation will reveal if Mg segregates to grain boundaries and triggers localized compound formation that compromises passivation. The hypothesis predicts that distinct intermetallic phases will appear above a specific exposure temperature–time product, degrading corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-processed state. If such transformations do not occur under these conditions, or if properties improve rather than degrade, then the hypothesis is falsified. This approach aligns with prior evidence of Mg-driven phase formation in Al–Mg LIGHT-CCAs and clarifies the role of metastable decomposition in service-relevant environments.
